title: Prompt Operator Mesh — design scratch
content:
Quick context: sketching a small, portable operator layer that sits between client SDKs and Redwood Inference endpoints. Purpose: declarative composition of prompt transforms, routing, fallback policies, and lightweight local caching. Target user: SDK authors, edge proxies, and partner integrations that need predictable runtime behavior without baking complex logic into every app.

Goals / constraints (notes to self):
- Small JSON/YAML config model that can be evaluated with minimal runtime (JS/Go/Rust).
- Deterministic execution order, first-class idempotency hooks, and stateless operator implementations where possible.
- Support hybrid routing: prefer local/private endpoint, fallback to hosted; optionally broadcast to an ensemble of models for reranking.
- Pluggable transforms: prompt_templates, instruction_sanitizers, safety_filters, hydration providers (e.g., embeddings + retrieval).
- Instrumentation hooks (trace ids, sampling) and lightweight telemetry events (operator start/end, duration).
- Policy-first: must be able to declare rate-limit/backoff and token-budget caps per-route.

High-level runtime diagram (ASCII):

Client SDK --> Operator Mesh Layer --> Router --> Redwood Endpoint(s)
                              |
                              +--> Local KV (prefix cache)
                              +--> Hydration service (embeddings/rag)

Operator Mesh Layer responsibilities:
- Parse a config bundle (versioned) associated with an API key or route.
- Execute operator pipeline (array) with short-circuit semantics.
- Provide context bag across operators: {user_id, trace_id, session_meta, budget_counters, cached_kv_refs}.
- Emit event log entries for each operator.

Operator model (primitive types):
- type: transform | route | preflight | postprocess | cache | policy
- id: short string
- config: opaque map (schema depends on operator type)
- on_error: continue | fail | fallback:<operator-id>
- timeout_ms (optional)

Example pipeline (pseudo-yaml inside string):
- id: sanitize
  type: transform
  config: {kind: "strip-sensitive", rules: ["emails", "credit-cards"]}
  on_error: fail

- id: embed-and-retrieve
  type: preflight
  config: {provider: "local-vec", top_k: 4, score_threshold: 0.7}
  on_error: continue

- id: compose-prompt
  type: transform
  config: {template: "system: {{system}}\nuser: {{user_input}}\ncontext: {{rag_snippets}}", template_vars_source: ["session_meta","preflight.embed_results"]}
  on_error: fail

- id: route-primary
  type: route
  config: {strategy: "prefer_dedicated", candidates: ["redwood-private:comet-1", "redwood-hosted:llama-large"], hedge: {enabled: true, latency_ms: 200}}
  on_error: fallback:route-secondary

- id: route-secondary
  type: route
  config: {strategy: "fallback_any", candidates: ["redwood-hosted:llama-medium"]}
  on_error: fail

- id: response-filter
  type: postprocess
  config: {safety: "allow-list-check", max_length: 1024}
  on_error: continue

Notes on route operator:
- Strategy semantics: prefer_dedicated tries candidates in order but can simultaneously open a hedged request per config. The operator should expose hints to higher-level tracer about hedging decisions and costs.
- Candidates are logical names (namespace:model-tag). The router uses a lookup map to resolve to actual endpoint URLs and auth tokens (kept in runtime config, not the mesh bundle).
- Each route operator runs within a budget token counter. If the counter would be exceeded, operator must either reduce max_tokens or trigger on_error.

Cache operator sketch:
- type cache 
- config: {mode: prefix|response, ttl_ms: 60000, key_expr: "hash(session_id + prompt.digest)", positive_ttl_ms: 60000, negative_ttl_ms: 15000}
- semantics: cache operator can be placed before route to return a cached response or after postprocess to store results. Must be idempotent-aware and store metadata about model-version used.

Policy operator (quota/backoff):
- config: {quota_per_minute: 1200, token_quota_per_minute: 250000, throttle_type: leaky_bucket}
- on throttle: either queue (with max_wait_ms) or fail-fast. The mesh should optionally shadow-throttle (accept requests but favor lower-cost route).

API shape (evaluation call) — top-level JSON fields we expect in SDK -> mesh:
- api_key: string
- route: string (logical route name)
- user_id: string
- session_id: string
- prompt_input: string or structured message array
- mesh_config_version: string (optional) -- runtime will fetch if absent
- flags: list[string] (e.g., ["no-cache","prefer-latency"]) 

Response shape from mesh -> client: {status, result, model_meta, events[]} encoded as simple JSON. Events are an array of short event records: {op_id, start_ms, end_ms, status, note}. Keep the shape small to avoid payload bloat.

Edge cases / open questions: 
- How to safely store secrets needed to call private endpoints? Mesh bundle should not embed tokens; runtime must provide a resolution map. But we need a bootstrap handshake: sdk requests mesh config + a signed config token from control plane? Need a short design for that.
- Can we allow user-defined JS transforms? Dangerous. Probably only allow sandboxed WASM or builtin ops to keep deploy size small.
- How to version operator schemas? Use semver-like version and include migration helpers. Mesh runtime should reject unknown operator types unless 'allow_unknown' flag is explicitly set by admin.
- Observability: keep per-request detailed events for sampled traces only. For high-traffic clients, default sampling 0.1%.

Mini implementation notes:
- JS runtime: implement operator registry (map of id -> fn(context, cfg) -> result). Each operator is synchronous or returns promise. Provide execution harness to enforce timeout_ms and on_error semantics.
- Go runtime: same but with context.Context and channels for hedging. Keep operator config as map[string]interface{} at runtime; provide typed helper builders.
- Small reference lib (npm) with a compile step that validates bundle and emits a minimized JSON bundle + checksums.

Testing / validation matrix:
- Unit tests for operator chaining, error propagation, and cache semantics.
- Load test routing decisions (simulate dedicated capacity drops and expect fallback within SLA).
- Fuzz transforms to detect information leak through template vars.

Todo (short):
- [ ] Draft proto/json schema for operator bundle (tighten field names).
- [ ] Write an example bundle for a RAG use-case with local vector store and host fallback.
- [ ] Spike hedged requests impl in Go (serve a simple route that proxies to two endpoints and returns earliest + annotated meta).
- [ ] Security review: secrets bootstrap and wasm sandboxing.

Random brainstorm ideas to capture:
- 'operator macros' — small named sub-pipelines that can be reused to keep bundles DRY.
- 'cost-sensitivity' attribute on transforms so editor tooling can show estimated token delta before deployment.
- 'dry-run' mode: evaluate transforms but don't actually call route; useful for validation and template testing.

Notes to self: keep this intentionally minimal for first pass. The biggest win is standardizing routing + caching semantics so SDKs don't need bespoke logic. Next iteration: map this onto Redwood's routing primitives (prefer_dedicated, capacity_tiers, model_variants) and align 'candidate' naming with platform model catalog.

-- end --
